questions.q: Who is William Somerset Maugham, and which two biographical facts from his early life most directly inform the autobiographical elements in "The Luncheon"?
questions.a: William Somerset Maugham (1874–1965) was a British playwright, novelist, and short story writer born in Paris to British parents; after his parents' deaths, he was raised in England by an uncle, studied medicine at St. Thomas's Hospital London, and qualified as a doctor before abandoning practice for writing. The two most relevant facts are: (1) his childhood in Paris explains the story's authentic Parisian setting and French cultural details, and (2) his medical training instilled the detached, diagnostic narrative voice that observes human foibles without sentimentality. A wrong answer that only lists his famous novels (Of Human Bondage, The Moon and Sixpence) reveals the student is recalling literary fame instead of connecting biography to textual strategy.

questions.q: Explain why the setting "Foyot's restaurant in Paris" and the currency "eighty gold francs" are not incidental details but structural constraints that shape the protagonist's every decision in the story.
questions.a: Foyot's was a high-end restaurant frequented by French senators, making it a space where social performance and financial display are mandatory—this forces the narrator into a performative generosity he cannot afford. Eighty gold francs represented his entire monthly budget; in 1920s Paris, a modest luncheon cost 15 francs, but caviare, salmon, asparagus, champagne, and peaches would multiply that tenfold, turning a social invitation into a financial crisis. The setting and currency together create a closed economic system where every menu choice is a calculation of survival versus dignity. A wrong answer that treats these as mere "background colour" reveals the student misses how setting functions as an active antagonist in Maugham's tightly plotted stories.

questions.q: Using the vocabulary preview box, match each word to the specific narrative moment it signals: "devastating passion," "mortifying," "ingratiating," "vindictive." Explain your reasoning for each match.
questions.a: "devastating passion" → the narrator's ironic description of the woman at forty: "a charming age, but not one that excites a sudden and devastating passion at first sight" (exposes his clinical detachment). "mortifying" → the moment the narrator realizes he may be ten francs short and contemplates faking a robbery: "It would be mortifying to find myself ten francs short" (captures social humiliation). "ingratiating" → the headwaiter's "ingratiating smile on his false face" when presenting the ruinous peaches (signals predatory service). "vindictive" → the narrator's closing confession: "I do not believe that I am a vindictive man" (frames the final revenge as cosmic justice). A wrong answer that defines words in isolation without anchoring them to textual moments reveals the student treats vocabulary as dictionary exercise rather than narrative signposting.

questions.q: Compare the narrative stance of "The Luncheon" (first-person retrospective, 20-year gap) with that of "The Necklace" by Maupassant (third-person omniscient). How does Maugham's choice of a first-person narrator who is also the protagonist-victim alter the reader's alignment with irony?
questions.a: Maugham's first-person retrospective narration creates dramatic irony through the gap between the young narrator's real-time panic ("panic seized me") and the older narrator's composed, even amused, recounting ("I have had my revenge at last"). The reader simultaneously experiences the past self's entrapment and the present self's ironic mastery. In contrast, Maupassant's third-person omniscient in "The Necklace" positions the reader outside both characters, making the irony structural (the necklace is paste) rather than experiential. Maugham's choice makes the reader complicit in the narrator's suffering and his delayed triumph—we feel the franc-counting anxiety, then share the complacency of the final revelation. A wrong answer that only identifies "first-person vs third-person" without analysing the temporal distance (20 years) and its effect on ironic tone reveals superficial understanding of narrative technique.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The 'Look for these expressions' vocabulary box in the NCERT edition functions as a thematic roadmap, not just a glossary." Support your evaluation with three specific word-to-theme connections.
questions.a: The claim is valid. Three word-to-theme connections: (1) "complacency" → the final sentence "observe the result with complacency" encapsulates the theme of delayed, detached revenge—the narrator's satisfaction is cold, not hot. (2) "caviare" → functions as a metonym for performative luxury; the woman's "I never mind caviare" exposes the theme of hypocrisy (she claims asceticism while consuming luxury). (3) "ingratiating" → the headwaiter's "ingratiating smile" embodies the theme of transactional social performance—service masked as warmth, mirroring the woman's friendship masked as exploitation. A wrong answer that treats the box as mere "difficult words" misses how Maugham's lexical precision makes vocabulary thematic evidence.

questions.q: Create a 50-word "pre-reading journal entry" from the perspective of the young narrator on the morning of the luncheon, incorporating at least three preview vocabulary words and revealing his financial anxiety without stating it directly.
questions.a: Sample entry: "Thursday looms. Foyot's. She writes 'little luncheon'—but I know the prices there. My eighty francs must stretch four weeks. A mutton chop, water, no coffee. If she orders caviare or champagne, I'll smile with ingratiating composure while mortifying calculations race. Devastating passion? Hardly. Just devastating arithmetic." A poor answer that writes a generic diary entry without vocabulary integration or subtextual anxiety reveals the student cannot yet use lexical anticipation as a comprehension scaffold.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: "Before You Read: Context and Background" is a preparatory literary analysis skill that equips students to activate prior knowledge, research historical-authorial context, identify genre conventions, and predict thematic concerns before engaging with a short story text, ensuring informed ______ rather than passive reading.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're meeting a friend at an expensive ______ you can't afford, but you're too polite to cancel—this is exactly the trap the young Maugham walks into.
What is "Before You Read? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: "Before You Read: Context and Background" is a preparatory literary analysis skill that equips students to activate prior knowledge, research historical-authorial context, identify genre conventions, and predict thematic concerns before engaging with a short story text, ensuring informed comprehension rather than passive reading.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Next, locate the setting: ______s Paris, Foyot's (a real senators' restaurant), and the franc's purchasing power—eighty francs was a month's survival budget.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently research and articulate the author's biographical relevance, the story's historical setting, genre markers, and key vocabulary meanings, then use these to formulate three specific, text-grounded predictions about plot, character dynamics, and thematic tension in "The Luncheon.".
